title: The Black Star: from St Ann's Bay to Talgarth Road
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: St Ann's Bay, the birth on Market Street
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the north coast of Jamaica, in the bay where Christopher Columbus lay marooned a year with two worm-eaten caravels four centuries earlier, a stonemason and a domestic servant have a son and name him Marcus Mosiah. The father is Malchus Garvey, a man who owns books, argues his own land cases, and loses them. The mother is Sarah Richards. Marcus is the youngest of their four; two of the four die in infancy. The marked birthplace is 32 Market Street, a few minutes' walk from the water. He will cross that water at twenty-two and go on crossing it for thirty years.
suggested_refs: The marked birthplace at 32 Market Street, St Ann's Bay, listed by the Jamaica National Heritage Trust
sources: Colin Grant, Negro with a Hat: The Rise and Fall of Marcus Garvey (2008), pp.8-9
Robert A. Hill (ed.), The Marcus Garvey and UNIA Papers, vol. 1

stops.name: St Ann's Bay, apprenticed at the godfather's press
stops.date_confidence: attested year; month and day not recorded, defaulted to January
stops.campa: At fourteen the boy is put to a trade. His godfather keeps a printing press in the town and takes him as apprentice, and Garvey learns type: the setting of it by hand, the weight of a forme, the arithmetic of a page. The popular chronologies send him to Kingston in this year. He does not go to Kingston. He goes across town, follows the press to its branch at Port Maria in 1904, and reaches the capital only in 1905. He keeps the trade for the rest of his life, and every organization he founds afterwards begins with a paper.
suggested_refs: The St Ann's Bay printing shop of Garvey's godfather, whose name the sources do not confirm
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, pp.13-16
Wikipedia, 'Marcus Garvey', Early career in Kingston: 1905-1909

stops.name: Kingston, the P. A. Benjamin works
stops.date_confidence: attested year; month and day not recorded, defaulted to January
stops.campa: At eighteen he comes down to Kingston and hires on at the P. A. Benjamin Manufacturing Company, whose printing serves a chemical and soap concern supplying half the island. He rises to master printer and foreman, the youngest in the shop. The city he enters is about to be levelled: the earthquake of 1907 takes down what the fire that follows does not. He reads the trade papers. The compositors count their wages against the price of bread, and the men who own the presses do not.
suggested_refs: The P. A. Benjamin Manufacturing Company works at Kingston, Garvey's first city employer
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, pp.13-16

stops.name: Kingston, the compositors strike
stops.date_confidence: attested month; day not recorded
stops.campa: His mother Sarah dies in March. In November the compositors of Kingston strike for wages, and Garvey, vice president of their section of the Printers' Union, leads them out. The strike breaks. Imported machinery does the work of the men, and the shops that reopen will not have him back on any terms. He finds work with a government printer, the only press on the island still willing to employ him, and begins to think about a paper of his own. The reference works date this strike to 1907, the year of the earthquake.
suggested_refs: The Printers' Union of Kingston and its compositors' section, whose strike of November 1908 Garvey helped lead
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, p.18

stops.name: Kingston, the National Club and the Watchman
stops.date_confidence: attested month for the National Club post; the paper is dated to 1910 without a month
stops.campa: Blacklisted from the private shops, he turns the trade outward. In April he is made assistant secretary of the National Club, the first Jamaican body to campaign against colonial rule, and in the same year he prints Garvey's Watchman, his own paper, which runs to three issues and stops. He is twenty-two and can set a page himself. What he cannot do is pay for the paper past its third issue. Nobody in Kingston with money to lend will lend it to a paper arguing against colonial rule.
stops.quote: If you have no confidence in self you are twice defeated in the race of life. With confidence you have won even before you have started.
stops.quote_source: Philosophy and Opinions of Marcus Garvey, ed. Amy Jacques Garvey (1923), Vol. I, Chapter I, 'Epigrams', p.12
suggested_refs: Garvey's Watchman, three issues, Kingston 1910; no surviving run located in the sources consulted
sources: Hill (ed.), The Marcus Garvey and UNIA Papers, vol. 1

stops.name: Puerto Limon, timekeeper on the banana works
stops.date_confidence: attested year; month inferred
stops.campa: He follows the labour south. On the Caribbean coast of Costa Rica the United Fruit Company grows bananas on land it holds outright and works them with West Indians who came for the wage and stay for want of the fare home. Garvey keeps the time book: he writes down the hours of men housed in barracks, paid in company scrip, buried where they fall. He petitions the British consul on their behalf and is told the men are not the consul's concern. In his own account of his life he dates the beginning of everything to this ledger.
suggested_refs: United Fruit Company plantation records for Limon Province, 1910, and Garvey's 1923 sketch 'The Negro's Greatest Enemy'

stops.name: Puerto Limon, the bilingual paper
stops.date_confidence: attested to spring 1911; day not recorded
stops.campa: In the spring he starts a paper of his own again, Nation in English and La Nacion in Spanish, printed for the plantation men and against the company that houses them. It runs until the press breaks. The part cannot be got on that coast and cannot be got from the capital, and the paper stops in the middle of its argument. He will found another at Colon. The press was bought cheap, the type stands half set in the case, and no money on that coast will finish either the repair or the argument.
suggested_refs: Nation / La Nacion, Puerto Limon, 1911, folded when the press could not be repaired
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, p.30

stops.name: Colon, the canal camps
stops.date_confidence: attested year; month inferred
stops.campa: At Colon, where the canal is being cut and the West Indians who dig it are counted separately in the payrolls and separately in the dead, he founds La Prensa and works the isthmus: Bocas del Toro by tradition, Ecuador by the record, ports where the same men from the same islands do the same work under different flags. He returns to Kingston in 1911 with a fever that nearly kills him, and with the conclusion that what he has been writing down is not local to any one coast.
suggested_refs: La Prensa, founded by Garvey at Colon, Panama, distinct from the earlier Limon paper with which it is often conflated
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, p.31

stops.name: Borough High Street, the room in Southwark
stops.date_confidence: attested to spring 1912; day not recorded
stops.campa: He sails for England in the spring and takes a room on Borough High Street, south of the river, not in the East End where the chronologies put him. He labours in the docks by the piece, sits in the public gallery of the House of Commons to watch an empire discuss itself, and speaks at Speakers' Corner to whoever stops. His sister Indiana joins him in August, five months after the accounts have them living together. London in 1912 is the head office of the thing he has been reading in ledgers at Limon and Colon, and he has come to look at it directly.
suggested_refs: Garvey's rented room on Borough High Street, Southwark, and the dock work he took by the piece in 1912
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, pp.35-36, 38, 45

stops.name: Fleet Street, the African Times and Orient Review
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1913-1914; month not recorded, defaulted to January
stops.campa: Duse Mohamed Ali, Egyptian, actor, journalist, pan-Africanist and pan-Islamist, edits the African Times and Orient Review off Fleet Street, and Garvey goes to work for him. He runs errands, he writes, and he watches a monthly report the whole colonized world to itself as a single subject: Egypt, India, the Gold Coast, the West Indies, one grievance in many languages. The Negro World will be built to this specification. He is twenty-five, and for the first time the press he works is arguing his case.
suggested_refs: The African Times and Orient Review, ed. Duse Mohamed Ali, London 1912-1920, template for the Negro World
sources: Ian Duffield, scholarship on Duse Mohamed Ali

stops.name: Fetter Lane, the evening class in law
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1913-14, month not recorded; the Bloomsbury campus given in the reference works is an anachronism, Birkbeck sat in the Breams Buildings on Fetter Lane until 1952
stops.campa: Two minutes' walk from the office, in the Breams Buildings on Fetter Lane, Birkbeck College teaches working men in the evenings, and Garvey enrolls for law. The reference works move this classroom to Bloomsbury, where the college goes in 1952, and add philosophy to the syllabus, which no source carries. What he takes from the class is procedural: how a charter is drawn, how a company is incorporated, how a man conducts a case in his own person. He will incorporate a shipping line on it, and ten years later he will defend himself with it.
suggested_refs: Birkbeck College in the Breams Buildings, Fetter Lane, its home from 1885 until the move to Malet Street in 1952
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, p.45

stops.name: Kingston, Orange Street, the association in a hotel room
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1914; the 1 August date carried in the reference works is not supported
stops.campa: He lands at Kingston in July and within the month founds the Universal Negro Improvement and Conservation Association and African Communities League, with himself as president and travelling commissioner. There is no hall. The association is run out of his hotel room on Orange Street until Amy Ashwood, who joins at the first meeting and argues him into it, gets headquarters on her father's credit. The programme is uplift, education, and a return to Africa on terms Africans set. Jamaica does not join in numbers.
stops.quote: Nationhood is the highest ideal of all peoples.
stops.quote_source: Philosophy and Opinions of Marcus Garvey (1923), Vol. I, Chapter I, 'Epigrams', p.11
suggested_refs: The founding constitution of the Universal Negro Improvement and Conservation Association and African Communities League, Kingston, July 1914
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, pp.53, 56

stops.name: Port of New York, the landing from the SS Tallac
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He comes ashore on the twenty-third of March to raise money for an industrial school in Jamaica on the Tuskegee model, meaning to stay a few months. Booker T. Washington, whose correspondence drew him, died the previous November, and the school is never built. Garvey finds instead a Harlem filling with West Indians and with southerners off the trains, and a street tradition of speaking to them from a ladder. His first attempt at it ends with the crowd heckling him and Garvey falling off the platform.
suggested_refs: The SS Tallac passenger manifest, New York, 23 March 1916
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, pp.72-73, 90

stops.name: Harlem, the New York branch
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1917; day not recorded
stops.campa: After a year on the road through thirty-eight states, sleeping in the houses of ministers and lodge men, he stops travelling and founds the New York division of the association. It begins with a handful of members in a rented room. Within two years it is the largest Black organization in the city, and the constitution he learned to draw in a Fetter Lane evening class is the instrument that holds it together, division by division, with dues and minutes and officers. He no longer speaks of a school in Jamaica.
stops.quote: The greatest weapon used against the Negro is DISORGANIZATION.
stops.quote_source: Philosophy and Opinions of Marcus Garvey (1923), Vol. I, Chapter I, 'Epigrams', p.12
suggested_refs: The charter and minute books of the New York division of the UNIA, founded May 1917
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, pp.87, 93

stops.name: Harlem, the platform with Hubert Harrison
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1917; the hall is not named in the sources consulted, so the pin is a general Harlem coordinate
stops.campa: Hubert Harrison, the Virgin Islander whom Harlem calls the father of its radicalism, opens the Liberty League of Negro-Americans and gives the new man from Jamaica the platform at the inaugural meeting. Garvey speaks and the hall goes to him. Harrison, who has the better library and the smaller voice, watches an audience he assembled leave behind somebody else, and writes about it afterwards with the precision of a man describing his own robbery. The two spend a decade in and out of each other's papers.
suggested_refs: The inaugural meeting of Hubert Harrison's Liberty League of Negro-Americans, Harlem, June 1917
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, pp.87, 93

stops.name: Harlem, the Negro World
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1918; the 1917 date in the popular chronologies is a year early
stops.campa: In April the association begins printing a weekly, the Negro World, and Garvey is back at the trade he learned at fourteen. It carries no advertisement for skin bleach or hair straightener, which costs it revenue and settles its argument in advance. Circulation nears ten thousand within a year, backed in part by Madam C. J. Walker, whose fortune was made in hair. The paper is banned in the colonies of several European powers and read aloud inside them anyway, by men who can read, to men who cannot.
stops.quote: Be as proud of your race today as our fathers were in the days of yore. We have a beautiful history, and we shall create another in the future that will astonish the world.
stops.quote_source: Philosophy and Opinions of Marcus Garvey (1923), Vol. I, Chapter I, 'Epigrams', p.11
suggested_refs: Bound runs of the Negro World, weekly from April 1918, and the colonial bans on its circulation
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, p.135

stops.name: 56 West 135th Street, the Black Star Line
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1919; the month is approximate
stops.campa: He incorporates a shipping company owned by Black shareholders and crewed by Black seamen, and sells the shares at five dollars each, door to door, to porters and laundresses and men off the docks, who pay in cash. The ships are to carry cargo and, in time, settlers to Liberia: the cape Robert Finley's American Colonization Society took in 1822 for a return organized by white men, now proposed on terms the settlers themselves set. Garvey never sets foot there. Joshua Milton Blahyi will fight over that ground.
stops.quote: The Negro must have a country and a nation of his own. If you laugh at the idea, then you are selfish and wicked, for you and your children do not intend that the Negro shall discommode you in yours.
stops.quote_source: Marcus Garvey, 'An Appeal to the Soul of White America' (2 October 1923), reprinted in Philosophy and Opinions, Vol. II (1925), pp.5-6
suggested_refs: Black Star Line stock certificates at five dollars a share, sold door to door from 56 West 135th Street
sources: robert_finley.journey.json, stop 'Monrovia, the settlers move onto the cape'

stops.name: Liberty Hall, 114 West 138th Street
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1919; day not recorded
stops.campa: The association buys a half-built church on 138th Street, roofs it, and names it Liberty Hall after the union hall in Dublin, because Garvey has been following the Irish. It seats six thousand. There are meetings nightly, a choir, a nurse corps, a legion in uniform, and a hierarchy of titles and sashes that the newspapers find comic and the members do not. Prince Hall chartered the first Black lodge in America on the same principle: an order of one's own, with its own regalia and its own minutes.
suggested_refs: Liberty Hall at 114 West 138th Street, dedicated July 1919, named for Liberty Hall in Dublin
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, pp.197-198

stops.name: 56 West 135th Street, the shots of George Tyler
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the fourteenth of October a man named George Tyler walks into the Black Star Line office, says he has been sent, and fires. Two shots take Garvey in the right leg and the scalp. Amy Ashwood puts herself between the two men and Tyler runs. Taken to the Harlem jail, he goes over the rail of the third tier almost at once, and no source ever records why he came or who, if anyone, sent him. Garvey addresses a meeting within days with his head bandaged, and the subscription taken that night is the largest yet.
stops.quote: Power is the only argument that satisfies man.
stops.quote_source: Philosophy and Opinions of Marcus Garvey (1923), Vol. I, Chapter II, 'Power', p.22
suggested_refs: New York Times reporting of the Tyler shooting, October 1919, and the Harlem jail inquest
sources: Contemporary New York Times reporting, October 1919

stops.name: Hudson River pier, the Yarmouth renamed
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Two weeks after the shooting the line's first ship is dressed with flags at a Hudson pier and renamed the Frederick Douglass. She is thirty years old, a coal-burning tramp, and thousands of people who have never owned anything at sea come down to the water to look at her. She needs eleven thousand dollars in repairs within weeks, calls first at Havana and then at Kingston, is towed home by the coastguard on her second voyage, and in 1922 is sold for scrap for less than a hundredth of her purchase price.
suggested_refs: The SS Yarmouth, renamed Frederick Douglass, launched with ceremony on the Hudson, 31 October 1919

stops.name: Liberty Hall, the Christmas marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On Christmas Day he marries Amy Ashwood, who founded the association with him in a Kingston hotel room five years earlier and who stepped in front of a gun for him in October. The ceremony is Catholic and private; the celebration at Liberty Hall runs to three thousand guests. The marriage lasts under three years. Ashwood contests the divorce he later obtains in Missouri for the rest of her life, calls herself his lawful wife in every city she lectures in, and outlives him by nearly thirty years.
suggested_refs: The Liberty Hall wedding celebration of 25 December 1919, attended by some three thousand
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, p.239

stops.name: Hudson River, the Shady Side excursions
stops.date_confidence: the deposit is attested to the first half of 1920; the July dating in the reference works belongs to another event, the dismissal of the line's secretary and captain
stops.campa: The line puts ten thousand dollars down on a paddle steamer, the Shady Side, and runs her up the Hudson on summer weekends with Harlem aboard: a band, a picnic, a river excursion on a boat the passengers hold shares in. She is the smallest vessel of the fleet and the one most of them ever actually board. Her boiler and her hull are older than the company that bought her, and by the end of the season she is beached on the New Jersey shore, having earned back less than the deposit.
suggested_refs: The paddle steamer Shady Side, bought on a ten thousand dollar deposit for Hudson excursions in 1920
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, p.233

stops.name: Harlem, the convention opens
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the first of August the First International Convention of the Negro Peoples of the World opens in Harlem, delegates from twenty-five countries in the hall, and for a month the streets carry parades: the African Legion, the Black Cross Nurses, the Motor Corps, the bands. A century earlier Robert Finley proposed from a Princeton study that free Black Americans be sent to Africa, for the good of the country that would not have them. The same return is argued in this hall, on the same continent, by the people who would be going.
stops.quote: Wake up Ethiopia! Wake up Africa! Let us work towards the one glorious end of a free, redeemed and mighty nation. Let Africa be a bright star among the constellation of nations.
stops.quote_source: Philosophy and Opinions of Marcus Garvey (1923), Vol. I, Chapter I, 'Epigrams', p.11
suggested_refs: The month-long First International Convention of the Negro Peoples of the World, Harlem, August 1920
sources: robert_finley.journey.json, stop 'Harlem, the return proposed on other terms'

stops.name: Madison Square Garden, the Declaration of Rights
stops.date_confidence: attested to the convention's Madison Square Garden session in August 1920; the building is Madison Square Garden II at Madison Avenue and 26th Street, not the Garden opened in 1925
stops.campa: Twenty-five thousand people fill the Stanford White Garden at Madison Avenue and 26th Street to adopt the Declaration of Rights of the Negro Peoples of the World and to hear Garvey named Provisional President of Africa. He holds no territory on the continent and has never seen it. Eighty-eight years later Muammar Gaddafi will have himself proclaimed King of Kings of Africa at Benghazi and chair a union pressing for a single African state. Gaddafi holds Libya. The single state is never formed.
stops.quote: If 400,000,000 Negroes can only get to know themselves, to know that in them is a sovereign power, is an authority that is absolute, then in the next twenty-four hours we would have a new race, we would have a nation, an empire, resurrected, not from the will of others to see us rise, but from our own determination to rise, irrespective of what the world thinks.
stops.quote_source: Philosophy and Opinions of Marcus Garvey (1923), Vol. I, Chapter III, 'Man Know Thyself', p.39
suggested_refs: The Declaration of Rights of the Negro Peoples of the World, adopted at Madison Square Garden II, August 1920
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, p.245
muammar_gaddafi.journey.json, stops 'Benghazi, King of Kings of Africa' and 'Addis Ababa, the African Union chair'

stops.name: New York, the arrest over the Orion
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1922, day not recorded; the indictment follows in February and the two events are commonly merged
stops.campa: In January he is arrested and charged with using the mails to defraud: a Black Star Line circular advertised shares in a ship called the Orion, which the line did not own. Bail is twenty-five hundred dollars, and the indictment follows in February. He has been arrested once already over these shares, at Chicago in 1919, under the state law against selling the blue sky, when the line had taken in some fifty thousand dollars. It has taken in a great deal more since, and every dollar was raised by advertisement.
stops.quote: I trust no one from the people would believe that I could be so mean as to defraud a fellow Negro, either directly or indirectly. I have an ideal that is far above money, and that is to see my people really free.
stops.quote_source: Philosophy and Opinions of Marcus Garvey (1923), Vol. I, Chapter V, 'Statement on Arrest', p.100
suggested_refs: The Black Star Line circular advertising shares in the SS Orion, a ship the line never owned

stops.name: Atlanta, the meeting with Edward Young Clarke
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1922; day not recorded
stops.campa: In June he goes to Atlanta and sits down with Edward Young Clarke, Imperial Wizard of the Ku Klux Klan, on the reasoning that the Klan states plainly what the whole country practises, and that two organizations which agree the races should live apart have business to transact. Officers of his own association resign over it. The Black press turns on him and does not turn back, and the campaign to have him prosecuted and deported is pressed hardest by his rivals in Harlem.
suggested_refs: The Atlanta meeting of June 1922 between Garvey and Klan Imperial Wizard Edward Young Clarke

stops.name: Baltimore, the marriage to Amy Jacques
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1922; day not recorded
stops.campa: In July he marries Amy Jacques, who has been his secretary, at Baltimore. The New York court has refused him a divorce from Amy Ashwood; he has taken one in Jackson County, Missouri, and its validity is disputed from the day it issues. Jacques edits the two volumes of his Philosophy and Opinions, runs the movement's correspondence while he is in prison, raises two sons, and writes the memoir that fixes his memory. Both wives are named Amy. Neither ever concedes the other's claim to him.
suggested_refs: The Jackson County, Missouri divorce decree, contested by Amy Ashwood for the rest of her life
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, p.239

stops.name: Park Row, the Federal Building
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1923, day not recorded; the Foley Square courthouse named in the reference works did not open until 1936, so the venue is the old Post Office and Federal Building at Broadway and Park Row
stops.campa: The trial opens in May in the old Post Office and Federal Building at Broadway and Park Row, before Judge Julian Mack. Garvey dismisses his counsel and conducts his own defence, which is the Fetter Lane evening class turned to account and turned against him: he cross-examines for weeks and addresses the jury on Africa. On the eighteenth of June he is convicted of using the mails to defraud and sentenced to five years and a thousand dollars. In September Judge Martin Manton admits him to bail at fifteen thousand.
suggested_refs: The trial record of United States v. Garvey, 1923, printed in the Garvey and UNIA Papers, vol. 5

stops.name: Atlanta, the federal penitentiary
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1925; day not recorded
stops.campa: The appeal fails and he is taken off a train at Atlanta and put inside the federal penitentiary on McDonough Boulevard. He has influenza in the infirmary and a bronchitis that never afterwards leaves him. He writes to the membership every week and the Negro World prints the letters; Amy Jacques carries the correspondence and brings out the second volume of his Philosophy and Opinions to pay for the appeal. He serves about half the five years. Outside, the association begins to come apart without him.
stops.quote: Should we not, therefore, turn our eyes towards Africa, our ancestral home and free it from the thraldom of alien oppression and exploitation?
stops.quote_source: Philosophy and Opinions of Marcus Garvey (1923), Vol. I, Chapter IV, 'The Slave Trade', p.46
suggested_refs: United States Penitentiary, Atlanta, 601 McDonough Boulevard SE, where Garvey was held February 1925 to November 1927

stops.name: New Orleans, the SS Saramaca
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: President Coolidge commutes the sentence on the eighteenth of November, to expire at once and on the condition that the man leaves the country. He is taken by train from Atlanta to New Orleans and put aboard the SS Saramaca on the third of December, deported as an undesirable alien. About a thousand people come down to the wharf to see him go. He has been in the United States eleven years, and the association he built there keeps its headquarters in Harlem. He never sees the country again.
suggested_refs: Coolidge's commutation of 18 November 1927, conditioned on immediate deportation
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, pp.410-411

stops.name: Cristobal, refused permission to land
stops.date_confidence: the call and the refusal are attested; the exact day is inferred, falling between 3 and 10 December 1927
stops.campa: The Saramaca puts in at Cristobal on the Panamanian isthmus, at the mouth of the canal, and the wharf fills: West Indians, the same men and the sons of the men whose hours he wrote into a time book. He asks permission to land. The authorities refuse it, and he speaks to the crowd from the ship. Sixteen years earlier he walked these camps unwatched, with a paper called La Prensa and no title at all. He is transferred to the SS Santa Maria for Kingston without setting foot on the isthmus.
suggested_refs: The Saramaca's call at Cristobal, December 1927, and the transfer to the SS Santa Maria for Kingston
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, pp.411, 413

stops.name: Kingston Harbour, the crowd on the wharf
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He comes into Kingston Harbour on the tenth of December and the town empties onto the wharf to meet him. The colony that would not join his association in 1914 receives him thirteen years later as a returning sovereign, not as a convicted man put off an American ship. He is forty. He is barred from the country where his organization lives, and the Negro World goes on printing in Harlem without him. What he can reach from this wharf is an island of a million people and the mails.
stops.quote: Day by day we hear the cry of "AFRICA FOR THE AFRICANS." This cry has become a positive, determined one. It is a cry that is raised simultaneously the world over, because of the universal oppression that affects the Negro.
stops.quote_source: Philosophy and Opinions of Marcus Garvey (1923), Vol. I, Chapter I, 'Epigrams', p.14
suggested_refs: Contemporary Jamaican press reports of Garvey's landing at Kingston, 10 December 1927
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, p.413

stops.name: Edelweiss Park, Cross Roads
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1928; month and day not recorded, defaulted to January
stops.campa: He takes a property at Cross Roads on the edge of Kingston, calls it Edelweiss Park, and makes it the headquarters of the association and the entertainment of the city at once: a meeting hall, an open-air theatre, a dance floor, a printing office. Sunday nights bring concerts, elocution contests and vaudeville turns, and between them Garvey speaks. Jamaica has no other place where a Black audience is addressed as a public. He runs a movement of two continents from a park with a stage in it.
suggested_refs: Edelweiss Park at Cross Roads, Kingston, UNIA headquarters and theatre from 1928 to the 1934 auction
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, p.433

stops.name: London, the Royal Albert Hall
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He sails for England in April and hires the Royal Albert Hall for the sixth of June, and speaks there on the government of Africa by Africans, in the capital of the empire that governs most of it. Sixteen years earlier he was labouring in these docks by the piece, lodging in a room on Borough High Street, and speaking at Speakers' Corner to whoever stopped. He comes back to the same city deported from another one, with an association in decline and a title no state recognizes, and takes for one evening the hall he could not have entered as a docker.
suggested_refs: Garvey's Royal Albert Hall address of 6 June 1928, the high point of the European tour
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, pp.422-425

stops.name: Paris, the city of the rival congress
stops.date_confidence: the 1928 visit is attested; the month and the itinerary within France are not recorded, so the date is inferred from the tour's sequence
stops.campa: From London he crosses to Paris, where in 1919 W. E. B. Du Bois convened a Pan-African Congress while the peacemakers sat at Versailles, and asked the powers to hold Africa in trust for its inhabitants. That is the rival tradition to his own and the older one. The two men have spent the decade since calling each other, in print, the greatest enemy the Negro has, and they want the same continent returned to the same people. Garvey passes through the city on his way to Geneva and neither man seeks the other.
suggested_refs: The Pan-African Congress convened by W. E. B. Du Bois at Paris in 1919, the rival programme to the UNIA's
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, pp.422-425

stops.name: Palais Wilson, the petition to the League
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1928; day not recorded
stops.campa: At Geneva he lays before the League of Nations a petition on behalf of the Negro peoples of the world, asking that the former German colonies in Africa be placed in Black hands rather than distributed as mandates among the victors. It is the association's second approach: five delegates were sent in 1922 and came back with nothing. The petition is formally received, and filed, and no action follows, and the mandates run on until other wars end them.
stops.quote: I know no national boundary where the Negro is concerned. The whole world is my province until Africa is free.
stops.quote_source: Philosophy and Opinions of Marcus Garvey (1923), Vol. I, Chapter III, p.37
suggested_refs: The UNIA petitions to the League of Nations, Geneva, 1922 and 1928, in the League archives
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, pp.340-341, 422-425

stops.name: Edelweiss Park, the People's Political Party
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1929, month approximate; History.com dates the founding to 1928 and the disagreement is left standing
stops.campa: He founds the People's Political Party at Edelweiss Park, the first modern political party in Jamaica, on a manifesto of fourteen planks: a minimum wage, an eight-hour day, land reform, a university for the island, legal aid for the poor, and the impeachment of judges who abuse their office. The last plank is read in court as contempt. He is tried, pleads guilty to demeaning the judiciary, serves three months in Spanish Town prison with a fine of a hundred pounds, and loses his Kingston council seat.
suggested_refs: The fourteen-plank manifesto of the People's Political Party, Jamaica's first modern party, 1929
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, pp.428-429

stops.name: Spanish Town Road, the election lost
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1930 Legislative Council election; the campaign has no single date, and the month is defaulted
stops.campa: He carries the party through the Legislative Council election and loses. The reason is not the conviction, which the chronicles blame: it is the franchise. Jamaica gives the vote by property and by income, and the men and women who fill Edelweiss Park on a Sunday night hold neither in the amounts required. He can put ten thousand people in a park and cannot put a tenth of them on the register. Universal adult suffrage comes to Jamaica in 1944, four years after his death.
suggested_refs: The property and income qualifications governing the Jamaican franchise at the 1930 Legislative Council election
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, p.429

stops.name: Edelweiss Park, the Coronation of an African King
stops.date_confidence: attested to August 1930; day not recorded
stops.campa: In August he stages his own play at the park theatre, the Coronation of an African King, three months before Ras Tafari is crowned Haile Selassie at Addis Ababa. Jamaica reads that coronation through Garvey's argument, and out of the reading comes a religion he never founds and never accepts, which takes him for its prophet and the emperor for its god. In 1935 Benito Mussolini invades Ethiopia and drives the emperor into exile, and the faith that began at this stage becomes worldwide.
suggested_refs: Garvey's play Coronation of an African King, staged at the Edelweiss Park theatre, August 1930
sources: Barry Chevannes, Rastafari: Roots and Ideology (1994)
mussolini.journey.json, stops 'Rome, Palazzo Venezia, war declared on Ethiopia' and 'Rome, Palazzo Venezia, empire proclaimed'

stops.name: Beaumont Crescent, West Kensington
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1935; day not recorded
stops.campa: Edelweiss Park is foreclosed and auctioned in 1934, and in March he sails for London and rents in West Kensington, setting up the association's headquarters on Beaumont Crescent. He publishes a monthly, The Black Man, largely written by himself. The Harlem division has broken from him, the Negro World has stopped printing, and the movement that once counted its members in millions is run out of a rented room by a man in his late forties who answers the letters in his own hand. He does not go back to Jamaica.
suggested_refs: The UNIA headquarters on Beaumont Avenue and Crescent, West Kensington, and the monthly magazine The Black Man
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, pp.433, 438, 444

stops.name: Toronto, the School of African Philosophy
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1937 UNIA convention at Toronto, month approximate; the venue named in the reference works is unverified and no hall is asserted here
stops.campa: The annual convention meets at Toronto and Garvey crosses to it, then stays to teach a course he calls the School of African Philosophy: leadership, elocution, personality, the sciences of organization, examined and graded, the lessons mailed to students who cannot attend. He returns for the convention of the following summer. It is the last large audience he addresses. Ten years earlier he sold them shares in ships; now he mails them lessons and marks the papers himself.
suggested_refs: The lessons of Garvey's School of African Philosophy, taught at Toronto in 1937 and mailed to correspondence students
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, pp.442, 444

stops.name: 53 Talgarth Road, the last house
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1937; month and day not recorded, defaulted to October after the Toronto return
stops.campa: He takes a family house at 53 Talgarth Road in West Kensington, on the road running west out of London, and lives there with his wife and sons and then alone, when Amy Jacques takes the boys home to Jamaica. He writes, he answers correspondence from divisions in six countries, and he tells visitors the movement is not finished. The house is the last address of an organization that once owned ships. In 2005 a blue plaque goes up on the front of it, four of its words doing the work: lived and died here.
suggested_refs: The blue plaque installed at 53 Talgarth Road in 2005, reading that Garvey lived and died here
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, pp.438, 444

stops.name: Talgarth Road, the obituaries
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In January a stroke leaves him largely paralysed. In late May the papers print his obituary, on a rumour traced to George Padmore, and the notices are unkind: dead, they say, broke, alone and unpopular. He has them read to him. On the second day of the reading a second stroke comes, massive, and two weeks after that, on the tenth of June, he dies in the house on Talgarth Road at fifty-two. Whether the obituaries killed him is a thing his biographers repeat and cannot demonstrate.
stops.quote: Let Africa be our guiding Star, OUR STAR OF DESTINY.
stops.quote_source: Philosophy and Opinions of Marcus Garvey (1923), Vol. I, Chapter I, 'Epigrams', p.11
suggested_refs: The premature obituaries of May 1940 and the British press notices of Garvey's death on 10 June
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, pp.1-2, 448-450

stops.name: St Mary's, Kensal Green, the vault in the catacombs
stops.date_confidence: the burial is attested to June 1940; the day is not recorded in the sources consulted and is defaulted
stops.campa: He is laid in a vault in the catacombs beneath the chapel of St Mary's Roman Catholic Cemetery at Kensal Green, in a London at war, with no possibility of carrying a body across the Atlantic. The provisional president of a continent he never saw lies in the northwest of the imperial capital, a few miles from the docks where he laboured by the piece in 1912. He stays there twenty-four years. Jamaica is still a colony on the day he is buried, and comes for him only after it is not.
suggested_refs: St Mary's Roman Catholic Cemetery, Kensal Green, and the chapel catacomb vault that held Garvey until 1964
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, p.451

stops.name: National Heroes Park, the reburial
stops.date_confidence: attested; the reference chronologies give 13 November and an undated November, and both are wrong
stops.campa: Independent Jamaica sends for the body in November 1964. It lies in state in the Catholic cathedral at Kingston and is reinterred on the twenty-second in what is then King George VI Memorial Park, in a tomb at the centre of a raised platform built in the shape of a black star, with a bust by Alvin Marriott that has stood on the ground since 1956. The Order of the National Hero is conferred on him in 1969, the first of them, and the style he carries is the Right Excellent.
stops.quote: There is always a turning point in the destiny of every race, every nation, of all peoples, and we have come now to the turning point of the Negro, where we have changed from the old cringing weakling, and transformed into full-grown men, demanding our portion as MEN.
stops.quote_source: Philosophy and Opinions of Marcus Garvey (1923), Vol. I, Chapter I, 'Epigrams', p.12
suggested_refs: The Garvey shrine at National Heroes Park, Kingston, designed by G. C. Hodges in the shape of a black star
sources: Grant, Negro with a Hat, p.454
